subject: ventures/insurance-agency-book-valuation-calculator
professional: an insurance-agency M&A broker / valuation analyst who prices independent-agency books; they check first (1) normalized earnings: is the owner's own labour costed at market so margin is a realistic 20-35% EBITDA rather than 75%, (2) the retention history and how the purchase-price true-up works (dollar-for-dollar shortfall at the multiple, measured over the holdback period), (3) the deal structure: cash at close vs holdback vs multi-year earn-out / pay-as-you-go, (4) the resulting multiple against market ranges (roughly 1.5-3x revenue for small books, 6-10x+ EBITDA for agencies), and (5) after-tax proceeds (capital-gain sale vs ordinary-income commissions)

Compared with node runs of analyze() (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/445518b1-5429-5297-9052-042574ff3b55/scratchpad/ins/run.mjs). Sample book (250k, 90%, 25% servicing, 15%, 15 y, 1.5x offer, 70% upfront, 12 m, 90% required, 3% costs): keep $657,920.55 both; offer value $349,076.09 both; break-even 2.8271x both; one more point $31,785.25 both. Variant at 81% retention: keep $444,364.08 and offer $339,293.48 both, holdback factor 0.9. CSV rows (year 1: 225,000 / 168,750 / 146,739) match the hand schedule. The arithmetic of the stated model is right to the cent; the score is not 4 because the stated holdback rule departs from deal practice (see domain) and the retention test ignores the holdback period.

Six hand-seeded mutations in calc.mjs, each reverted with git checkout -- calc.mjs and git status clean afterwards: 4 caught (costs on upfront only: 1 fail; holdback factor squared: 1 fail; keepValue horizon n-1: 2 fail; holdback discount months/24: 1 fail), 2 survived (onePoint step 0.01 -> 0.001, i.e. the headline 'one more point of retention' figure off by 10x, survives because calc.test.mjs:66 only asserts onePoint > 0; holdback-cut finding condition < -> <= survives because no test checks when that finding fires). Several caught mutations are caught by a single test. Expected values are the author's own hand calculations; no outside reference figures.

Pure dependency-free core, innerHTML writes go through esc() or numeric formatters, validation names each field. Defects: blank fields silently take defaults (num(v,d) at calc.mjs:16: blank retention becomes 90%, blank servicing 0%, blank required return 15%) with no notice; '$250k' is rejected with 'must be more than zero' rather than a parse message; retention 120% with 0% rate over 40 years returns $1.65 billion on a $250k book without warning beyond the generic >100% note; dead svg/.legend CSS (index.html:44-45) for a chart that does not exist.
evidence.claims: Checked: the How-it-is-calculated text matches calc.mjs line by line (revenue x retention^t, margin, discounting, min(1, exp/req) holdback, costs on the whole price); Not-modelled list (taxes, contingent commissions, earn-outs, transition, E&O) present on page, README and FAQ; 'Unverified: checked by hand calculation and unit tests only' is honest; disclaimer on page and README; privacy claim backed (page.test.mjs asserts no fetch/XHR/sendBeacon; grep of index.html confirms; usage.mjs localStorage only, DNT/GPC honoured). Source llms.txt points at duncan-haywood.github.io but the served llms.txt carries marisstella.app (source-only, not filed). One loose claim: the no-offer break-even finding says 'A buyer using the same inputs can pay up to about this much and still earn the required return' (calc.mjs:122), but the break-even is computed from the seller's holdback factor and seller transaction costs, not a buyer's cash flows.
evidence.fitness: Walked a selling agent's job: 250k book, an offer of 1.5x with 30% held back 12 months. The tool says keeping is worth $657,921 and the offer $308,844 less, break-even 2.83x. A broker would object in the first hour: the sample's 25% servicing and 0% payout leave a 75% margin with the owner's own labour uncosted (a normalized agency EBITDA margin is more like 20-35%), which is what pushes the break-even above typical small-book multiples; the holdback cut is proportional rather than the dollar-for-dollar true-up most agreements use; there is no multi-year pay-as-you-go / earn-out schedule (common for book sales), no after-tax comparison (sale proceeds often capital gain vs commissions as ordinary income), and no EBITDA-multiple view. The page states most of these limits, so the tool is honest, but the headline answer can steer a seller to reject a market-rate offer.
evidence.domain: Compared with agency M&A practice: purchase-price true-ups are typically dollar-for-dollar: price = multiple x revenue retained at the measurement date, so a shortfall below the threshold costs multiple x lost revenue. At 81% vs 90% required on the sample, the tool cuts the $112,500 holdback by $11,250 (factor 0.9); a dollar-for-dollar true-up cuts $33,750 (offer value $339,293 vs $319,728). The retention test also ignores the holdback period: a 24-month holdback with 90% annual retention is measured at 90%, not the 81% of base revenue actually retained after two years (tool $336,316 vs true-up $310,796). Valuation as discounted retained cash flow is a legitimate income approach, and showing keep value as revenue and cash multiples is useful, but no market-multiple cross-check and no owner-comp normalization.

defects.what: Holdback cut is proportional (min(1, expected/required)) rather than the dollar-for-dollar true-up at the multiple that agency purchase agreements typically use; at 81% vs 90% the tool cuts the $112,500 holdback by $11,250 instead of $33,750, overstating the offer by ~$19.6k PV.

Retention test ignores the holdback period: annual retention is compared directly with the required level, so a 24-month holdback at 90%/yr (81% of base retained) is paid in full; offer overstated ($336,316 vs ~$310,796).

Owner's own labour is not costed: with the sample's 0% payout and 25% servicing the book runs at a 75% margin, giving keep 2.63x revenue and a 2.83x break-even, which steers the headline finding ('offer is $308,844 below keeping') against a market-rate 1.5x offer; no normalized-EBITDA or market-multiple cross-check.
Two seeded mutations survive: the headline one-point-of-retention value can be off 10x (test only asserts > 0), and the holdback-cut finding's trigger is untested.

No multi-year pay-as-you-go / earn-out tranches and no after-tax comparison (capital-gain sale vs ordinary-income commissions); stated as not modelled, but these are the common structures for book sales.
Blank fields silently take defaults (blank retention 90%, servicing 0%, required return 15%); '$250k' is reported as revenue not above zero.

No-offer break-even finding claims a buyer 'can pay up to about this much and still earn the required return', but the figure uses the seller's holdback factor and transaction costs, not a buyer's cash flows.
Dead svg / .legend CSS for a chart the page does not have.

verdict: A small, honest, correctly-implemented discounted-cash-flow keep-vs-sell calculator: five independent recomputations (keep value, offer value, break-even, one-point value, 81% variant) match to the cent, the page states its model and limits, and privacy holds. It misses the bar on verification (2 of 6 seeded mutations survive, including a 10x error in the headline one-point figure) and falls short of what an agency M&A broker would sign off: the holdback is cut proportionally rather than dollar-for-dollar, the retention test ignores the holdback period, and the sample's uncosted owner labour (75% margin) makes a market-rate 1.5x offer look $309k too low. Finished (completeness 3), not at the bar.
